term_swaps.feedback: Ionic bonding involves electron transfer; covalent bonding involves sharing pairs of electrons.
Covalent bonding shares electrons; ionic bonding transfers electrons between ions.
At the anode, oxidation occurs; reduction occurs at the cathode.
Reduction happens at the cathode; oxidation happens at the anode.
Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings; endothermic reactions take energy in.
Endothermic reactions absorb energy from the surroundings; exothermic reactions release energy.
Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons; alkenes contain a carbon–carbon double bond.
Alkenes are unsaturated; alkanes have only single C–C bonds.
Acids have pH below 7; alkalis have pH above 7.
Alkalis are bases that dissolve in water; acids produce H⁺ ions in aqueous solution.
Protons are positively charged and in the nucleus; neutrons have no charge.
Neutrons have no charge; protons are positively charged.
Electrons are in shells around the nucleus; neutrons are in the nucleus.
A molecule contains two or more atoms chemically bonded together.
A compound contains atoms of different elements chemically combined.
An element contains only one type of atom.
Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain of electrons.
Reduction is gain of electrons; oxidation is loss of electrons.

options.text: The mass number is the number of protons only
options.feedback: Mass number is protons plus neutrons in the nucleus.

options.text: Electrons have a positive charge
options.feedback: Electrons are negatively charged; protons are positive.

options.text: All atoms of an element must have the same number of neutrons
options.feedback: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

options.text: The nucleus contains electrons in shells
options.feedback: Electrons occupy shells outside the nucleus; the nucleus contains protons and neutrons.

options.text: Atomic number counts protons and neutrons together
options.feedback: Atomic number is the number of protons only.

options.text: Elements in the same group have the same number of electron shells
options.feedback: Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in the outer shell.

options.text: Reactivity of Group 1 metals decreases down the group
options.feedback: Group 1 metals become more reactive down the group.

options.text: Noble gases react easily because they have a full outer shell
options.feedback: Noble gases are unreactive because they already have a full outer shell of electrons.

options.text: All metals are more reactive than all non-metals
options.feedback: Reactivity depends on the element and reaction — compare specific metals and non-metals.

options.text: Ionic compounds share pairs of electrons between atoms
options.feedback: Ionic bonding involves transfer of electrons to form ions; sharing is covalent bonding.

options.text: Covalent bonds form when a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal
options.feedback: That describes ionic bonding between metals and non-metals.

options.text: Ionic compounds conduct electricity well as solids
options.feedback: Ionic compounds conduct when molten or dissolved in water — not as solid crystals.

options.text: A covalent bond is a weak force between separate molecules
options.feedback: That describes an intermolecular force; covalent bonds hold atoms together in a molecule.

options.text: Ions in an ionic lattice are neutral particles
options.feedback: Ions have charge; the compound is neutral overall because positive and negative charges balance.

options.text: Simple covalent substances have high melting points because covalent bonds are strong
options.feedback: Simple molecules have weak intermolecular forces — it is these that melt, not the covalent bonds.

options.text: Diamond conducts electricity because it contains delocalised electrons
options.feedback: Diamond does not conduct — each carbon is bonded to four others with no free electrons.

options.text: Graphite is soft because it has weak covalent bonds between carbon atoms
options.feedback: Graphite is soft because layers slide over each other; covalent bonds within layers are strong.

options.text: Polymers are small molecules with low melting points
options.feedback: Polymers are large macromolecules; many have high melting points due to strong bonds.

options.text: One mole of any substance always has a mass of 1 g
options.feedback: The mass of one mole depends on relative formula mass — it is not always 1 g.

options.text: Concentration is measured in moles per cubic centimetre only
options.feedback: Concentration is often mol/dm³; check units carefully in calculations.

options.text: The relative formula mass is the mass of one atom of the substance
options.feedback: Relative formula mass compares to carbon-12; it relates to one mole of particles.

options.text: Avogadro's constant is the number of grams in one mole
options.feedback: It is the number of particles in one mole (about 6 × 10²³), not a mass.

options.text: All acids must contain oxygen in their formula
options.feedback: Acids produce H⁺ ions in aqueous solution — they do not have to contain oxygen.

options.text: Neutralisation produces only water
options.feedback: Neutralisation of an acid and alkali also produces a salt.

options.text: A solution with pH 7 is always a strong acid
options.feedback: pH 7 is neutral; acids have pH below 7.

options.text: Alkalis release hydrogen ions in water
options.feedback: Alkalis produce hydroxide ions (OH⁻) in aqueous solution.

options.text: Strong acids are always more concentrated than weak acids
options.feedback: Strength and concentration are different — a dilute strong acid can be less concentrated than a concentrated weak acid.

options.text: Positive ions move to the anode during electrolysis
options.feedback: Positive ions (cations) move to the cathode; anions move to the anode.

options.text: Electrolysis can occur in solid ionic compounds without melting them
options.feedback: Ionic compounds must be molten or in solution so ions are free to move.

options.text: At the cathode, negative ions lose electrons
options.feedback: Negative ions move to the anode where they lose electrons (oxidation).

options.text: The electrolyte is always a metal
options.feedback: The electrolyte is a molten or aqueous ionic compound that conducts.

options.text: Exothermic reactions do not need any energy to start
options.feedback: Activation energy is still needed to break bonds and start the reaction.

options.text: Endothermic reactions release thermal energy to the surroundings
options.feedback: Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings.

options.text: Breaking bonds releases energy overall
options.feedback: Breaking bonds requires energy; making bonds releases energy.

options.text: A reaction cannot be exothermic if the temperature falls
options.feedback: Some exothermic reactions feel cold if heat is absorbed from the surroundings to supply activation energy.

options.text: A catalyst is used up during a chemical reaction
options.feedback: Catalysts speed up reactions without being used up chemically.

options.text: Increasing temperature always decreases the rate of reaction
options.feedback: Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy — more frequent successful collisions.

options.text: Decreasing concentration always speeds up a reaction
options.feedback: Lower concentration means fewer particles per unit volume — fewer collisions per second.

options.text: A catalyst increases the yield of product at equilibrium
options.feedback: Catalysts increase rate of attainment of equilibrium but do not change the position of equilibrium.

options.text: At equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products are equal
options.feedback: At equilibrium, forward and reverse rates are equal — concentrations are not necessarily equal.

options.text: A reversible reaction stops when equilibrium is reached
options.feedback: Equilibrium is dynamic — both forward and reverse reactions continue.

options.text: Equilibrium can only be reached in an open system
options.feedback: A closed system is needed so substances cannot escape.

options.text: Alkenes are saturated hydrocarbons
options.feedback: Alkenes are unsaturated — they contain a C=C double bond.

options.text: Cracking always produces only smaller alkanes
options.feedback: Cracking can produce alkenes as well as smaller alkanes.

options.text: Complete combustion of hydrocarbons produces carbon monoxide and water only
options.feedback: Complete combustion produces carbon dioxide and water.

options.text: All fractions from crude oil have the same boiling point
options.feedback: Fractional distillation separates fractions with different boiling points.

options.text: Polymers are always made from many different types of monomer
options.feedback: Addition polymers are made from one type of alkene monomer repeated.

options.text: Condensation polymerisation produces only the polymer with no other products
options.feedback: Condensation polymerisation also produces a small molecule such as water.

options.text: All plastics are biodegradable
options.feedback: Many common plastics are not biodegradable and persist in the environment.

options.text: Rf value can be greater than 1.0 for a pure substance
options.feedback: Rf is always between 0 and 1 for a substance in a given solvent system.

options.text: A pure substance shows several spots on a chromatogram
options.feedback: A pure substance typically gives one spot (unless it decomposes).

options.text: The solvent front and the substance travel the same distance
options.feedback: Rf compares distance moved by substance to distance moved by solvent front.

options.text: A more reactive metal can be displaced from its compound by a less reactive metal
options.feedback: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound.

options.text: All metals can be extracted by heating with carbon
options.feedback: Very reactive metals such as aluminium are extracted by electrolysis, not carbon reduction.

options.text: Rusting is the reaction of iron with nitrogen in the air
options.feedback: Rusting involves iron reacting with oxygen and water.

options.text: Fuel cells store chemical energy like a rechargeable battery
options.feedback: Fuel cells are supplied continuously with fuel; they do not store energy like a battery.

options.text: In a hydrogen fuel cell, hydrogen is burned in a flame to produce electricity
options.feedback: A fuel cell uses an electrochemical reaction, not combustion in a flame.

options.text: All metals are renewable resources because they can be recycled
options.feedback: Metal ores are finite; recycling reduces demand but does not make ores renewable.

options.text: An alloy is a compound with a fixed ratio of metal and non-metal atoms
options.feedback: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements.

options.text: Corrosion of iron can be prevented only by painting
options.feedback: Sacrificial protection, galvanising, and alloying can also prevent rusting.
